analysis.one_liner: Makes it far easier to win monopoly lawsuits and largely bans acquisitions by giant digital companies worth over $100 billion.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal antitrust law to make it much easier to sue and win against monopolies. Plaintiffs would no longer have to define the market or prove market share — showing substantial market power or anticompetitive effects would be enough, and the company would have to prove its conduct was procompetitive by clear and convincing evidence. Courts would have to order violators to give up all profits earned from the illegal conduct. Companies worth more than $100 billion would be barred from acquisitions that may lessen competition, and the FTC could designate "dominant digital firms" whose acquisitions over $1 million are presumed to be unfair trade practices, while also requiring platforms to disclose when their search results favor their own businesses. The bill never advanced past introduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers and small businesses that compete against dominant platforms. Easier monopoly lawsuits, forced disgorgement of illegal profits, and near-bans on acquisitions by trillion-dollar-scale firms would make it harder for the largest tech companies to buy rivals and harder for them to favor their own products in search results. Small firms would be more likely to survive as independent competitors rather than sell out or be crushed.

how_it_helps.text: It lets an antitrust plaintiff win by showing substantial market power or anticompetitive effects — including with direct evidence — without having to define the market or prove the defendant's market share, removing a technical hurdle that has made monopoly cases hard to win.

It shifts the burden to the defendant: a company accused of monopoly conduct must prove by clear and convincing evidence that its procompetitive benefits outweigh the harm and that no less-risky alternative existed.
It requires courts to order companies that violate antitrust law in FTC or DOJ cases to give up all profits earned from the illegal conduct.

It bans companies worth over $100 billion from acquiring other firms where the deal may lessen competition, a direct attempt to stop the largest technology companies from buying rivals and nascent competitors.

It lets the FTC designate 'dominant digital firms' and presumes their acquisitions over $1 million are unfair trade practices, and requires platforms with search features to disclose when search results are promoted or demoted because they are affiliated with the platform.

analysis.who_pays: The largest corporations — chiefly the giant digital platforms — would bear the costs: losing the ability to freely acquire companies, surrendering all profits earned through antitrust violations, and facing FTC designation with special restrictions. Some consumers might also lose products or features that only large acquisitions could produce, and small startup founders would have one fewer exit path.

drawbacks.text: The bill lowers the evidentiary bar for plaintiffs and shifts the burden onto defendants to prove their conduct is procompetitive by clear and convincing evidence — a standard courts use for serious allegations — which critics of similar proposals argue could chill legitimate business practices and pro-competitive acquisitions that lower prices or improve products.

The $1 million presumption would treat nearly any acquisition by a designated dominant digital firm — including small startups that founders often want to sell — as an unfair practice by default, which could cut off a common path for new companies to grow and for investors to be repaid.

Allowing plaintiffs to skip defining the relevant market removes the framework courts have used for decades to distinguish competitive from anticompetitive conduct, and the FTC's unilateral power to designate firms as 'dominant digital firms' would subject targeted companies to special rules based on an agency determination.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The ideas the bill proposed — easing the plaintiff's burden to prove monopoly power, forcing dominant firms to justify conduct, forcing them to disgorge illegal profits, and presumptively blocking big acquisitions — are aggressive, and the specific mechanisms carry real risks: a presumption that almost any acquisition by a designated firm is unlawful could stop deals that genuinely benefit consumers, and dropping the market-definition step would make antitrust cases harder to defend against. But those are design questions Congress could have tested through hearings and amendment. Because the bill never got any committee consideration, no one had to defend or fix its weaknesses; the cost to the public is simply that the debate over whether big digital platforms face real antitrust limits did not happen in this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on April 12, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill received no further action — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large technology companies, which faced no new antitrust restrictions as a result. The bill's proposals to ease monopoly lawsuits and restrict big acquisitions were never adopted.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; it never left committee.

against.name: Large technology companies and their lobbying operations
against.role: Major tech firms (Amazon, Google, Apple, Facebook/Meta)
against.what_they_did: Ran extensive lobbying campaigns against antitrust legislation targeting dominant digital platforms during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator — a Republican — sponsored the bill, and no other member of either party signed on, so no party bloc ever took a recorded position.

industries.industry: Large technology platforms (search, social media, e-commerce)
industries.note: The bill is built around them: firms worth over $100 billion would face a near-ban on acquisitions, and the FTC could designate dominant digital firms whose deals over $1 million are presumed unlawful and whose self-preferencing search results must be disclosed. Their ability to buy rivals and steer users to their own services would shrink sharply.

Startups would find it much harder to sell to a large incumbent buyer, cutting off a common path for founders and investors to cash out. Some would benefit from a market less dominated by a few platform giants.

industries.industry: Small businesses, advertisers, and app developers
industries.note: These firms compete with or depend on dominant platforms; stricter antitrust enforcement and disclosure of self-preferencing search practices could give them a fairer competitive environment.

industries.industry: Antitrust plaintiffs' bar and enforcement agencies
industries.note: Easier evidentiary standards, mandated profit disgorgement, and the FTC's new designation power would expand the reach and success rate of antitrust cases.
